# Here Be Dragons

In the New York Public Library, in a climate-controlled room, there rests a small copper globe about the size of a grapefruit. It was cast in Europe sometime in the first decade of the sixteenth century, which makes it one of the oldest surviving globes on Earth — an artifact from the precise historical moment when it occurred to people that you could hold the whole world in two hands. The continents on it are sketchy and wrong in fascinating ways. And off the coast of Southeast Asia, pressed into the metal, runs a short Latin sentence: *HC SVNT DRACONES*. Here be dragons.

We carry around a mental image of old maps as crawling with that phrase — every blank ocean labeled with a warning. The truth is stranger and better: those words, in that form, appear on this globe and, as far as anyone has ever found, nowhere else. Old charts certainly bristle with sea monsters — whales like floating islands, serpents coiled in the waves — but the famous sentence itself seems to have been uttered exactly once, by one anonymous engraver, five centuries ago. All the dragons of cartography descend from a single animal. What I love about that globe isn't the dragon, though, but the gesture: the admission that a map can have an edge, a place where knowledge runs out and imagination clocks in for its shift.

Humans were drawing maps long before there were globes. The oldest surviving world map is a clay tablet you could rest in your palm, made in Babylon roughly twenty-six centuries ago. It shows the world as a disc: Babylon a small rectangle at the center, the Euphrates flowing down through it, everything ringed by a circular ocean labeled the Bitter River, with a few triangles jutting beyond the rim for distant lands no one from the city had ever seen. Every map begins exactly there — with the maker standing in the middle, working outward toward the unknown.

And yet the audacity came early. Around 240 BC, in Alexandria, Eratosthenes heard that in the southern city of Syene, at noon on the summer solstice, the sun shone straight down a well and cast no shadow at all. In Alexandria, that same noon, a stick cast a shadow of about seven degrees — one-fiftieth of a circle. The distance between the cities was known to the walkers who measured such things; multiply by fifty and you have the circumference of the Earth. He got roughly 250,000 stadia, which is somewhere between a hair and a sixth of the true figure, depending on whose stadion you trust. Either way, consider the nerve of it: a man with a stick and a shadow, wrapping his mind around a planet no one had ever seen whole.

For most of mapmaking history, the blanks were the best part. Joseph Conrad knew it. In *Heart of Darkness*, Marlow recalls being a boy with a passion for maps, losing himself in the glories of exploration, putting a finger on the empty middle of Africa — the biggest, the most blank — and declaring: when I grow up, I will go there. By the time Marlow tells the story, the patch has filled in with rivers and lakes and names. "It had ceased," he says, "to be a blank space of delightful mystery — a white patch for a boy to dream gloriously over."

It is worth pausing there, because the white patch was never white. The filling-in of maps was also a claiming. In the winter of 1884, men in overcoats sat around a table in Berlin and drew borders across Africa with rulers — straight lines laid over watersheds, grazing routes, and homelands that no one at the table had ever walked. Those lines still run through the politics of a continent. A map is a wonderful thing, but it has always been an instrument too: to chart a place is to tax it, administer it, own it. The dragon at the edge of the world was sometimes a flag waiting to be planted.

The last great blank wasn't on land at all. In the 1950s, an American cartographer named Marie Tharp sat in a lab at Columbia University inking the ocean floor by hand, plotting soundings brought back by research ships she was not, at first, permitted to sail on — women weren't. As the profiles accumulated, a shape kept insisting on itself: a deep valley running down the spine of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, like a wound along the seam of the world. Tharp suspected what it meant — that the seafloor was splitting apart there, being born. Her supervisor dismissed the idea as "girl talk." Years later, the painter Heinrich Berann would turn her work into the famous 1977 portrait of the world ocean floor: mountains, trenches, and that long wound of a valley, all of it resting on her patience.

Even now, the deeps keep their secrets.
